<context>
You are an expert at solving ARC-AGI (Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus) puzzles using Answer Set Programming (ASP).

ARC-AGI puzzles show input-output grid transformations. Each cell contains a color value (integer 0–9). The goal is to discover the hidden transformation rule from training examples and encode it as an ASP program.
</context>

<rules>
- `input(row, col, color)` facts are injected automatically — do not define them.
- `color(0..9)` facts are injected automatically — do not define them.
- the output predicate is always `output(row, col, color)` — do not redefine it.
- the final program must produce exactly one answer set, in which `output(row, col, color)` match the expected output exactly.
- end your program with `#show output/3.`
</rules>

<example_1>
This puzzle copies the input to the output unchanged.

<grid_1>
Input:
<diagram>
0 1 0
2 0 3
0 4 0
</diagram>

Output:
<diagram>
0 1 0
2 0 3
0 4 0
</diagram>
</grid_1>

<asp>
% Grid dimensions
n_rows(N) :- N = #count{ R : input(R, _, _) }.
n_cols(N) :- N = #count{ C : input(_, C, _) }.
row(0..N-1) :- n_rows(N).
col(0..M-1) :- n_cols(M).

% Output has the same dimensions as the input
output_cell(R, C) :- row(R), col(C).

% Each output cell gets exactly one color
1 { output(R, C, Color) : color(Color) } 1 :- output_cell(R, C).

% Copy each input cell to the output unchanged
output(R, C, Color) :- input(R, C, Color).

#show output/3.
</asp>
</example_1>

<asp>
% Grid dimensions

n_cols(N) :- N = #count{ C : input(_, C, _) }.
row(0..N-1) :- n_rows(N).
col(0..M-1) :- n_cols(M).

<asp>

% Define input dimensions
N = #count{R : input(R, _, _) }.
M = #count{C : input(_, C, _) }.
% Base dimension for output (depends on number of non‑zero cells)
D = N + M - 1.
% Number of non‑zero cells
K = #count{R, C : input(R, C, Color), Color != 0 }.
% Output grid size (square)
L = D * K.

% Define the rows and columns of the output grid
row(0..L-1) :- true.
col(0..L-1) :- true.
output_cell(R, C) :- row(R), col(C).

% Exactly one output color per cell
1 { output(R, C, Color) : color(Color) } 1 :- output_cell(R, C).

% Lower diagonal (keep original color) for every non‑zero cell
output(I, J, V) :- input(R, C, V), V != 0, row(I), col(J), I >= R, I >= C, J = L - 1 + C - I.

% Predicate for the same positions (used in constraints)
lower_diag(I, J) :- input(R, C, V), V != 0, row(I), col(J), I >= R, I >= C, J = L - 1 + C - I.

% Zero on the lower diagonal is forbidden – those cells must be non‑zero
:- output(I, J, 0), lower_diag(I, J).

% Non‑zero colors are forbidden for cells that are not on any lower diagonal
:- not lower_diag(R, C), output(R, C, Color), Color != 0.

% Optional: zeros on the upper diagonal (i + j = column) for zero cells
output(I, J, 0) :- input(R, C, 0), row(I), col(J), I >= R, I <= C, J = C - I.

#show output/3.
```

% Compute N, M, D, K, S

n_rows(N) :- N = #count{R : input(R, _, _) }.
n_cols(M) :- M = #count{C : input(_, C, _) }.
D = N + M - 1.
K = #count{R, C : input(R, C, Color), Color != 0 }.
S = D * K.

% Output dimensions
row(0..S-1) :- true.
col(0..S-1) :- true.
output_cell(R, C) :- row(R), col(C).

% Exactly one color per cell
1 { output(R, C, Color) : color(Color) } 1 :- output_cell(R, C).

% Index each non-zero input cell (lexicographic order)
idx(R_in, C_in, I) :- input(R_in, C_in, V_in), V_in != 0,
    I = #count{R2, C2 : input(R2, C2, V2), V2 != 0, (R2 < R_in) or (R2 = R_in and C2 < C_in)}.

% Output on diagonal cells:
output(R_out, C_out, V_in) :- idx(R_in, C_in, I), input(R_in, C_in, V_in), V_in != 0,
    R_out + C_out = S - 1 + I,
    row(R_out), col(C_out),
    R_out < S, C_out < S.

% Define diagonal cells predicate (any cell that has an output fact)
diag_cell(R, C) :- output(R, C, V), row(R), col(C), R < S, C < S.

% Forbid zero on diagonal cells
:- output(R, C, 0), diag_cell(R, C).

% Forbid non-zero on non-diagonal cells
:- not diag_cell(R, C), output(R, C, Color), Color != 0.

% (No need for other constraints; the rule already forces correct values on diagonal cells.)
